Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 75
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Cybersecurity Analyst
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure, Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish

Vignette:
Thuan Nguyen is a 75-year-old widower who works as a cybersecurity analyst, a role he has held for over three decades. He came to therapy at the urging of his adult daughter, who had grown concerned about his increasing isolation and the way he would become unreachable—staring blankly, his hands trembling—whenever she mentioned her own pregnancy. Thuan’s trauma began five years ago, when his youngest son, then thirty-two, was diagnosed with a rare and aggressive form of leukemia. The diagnosis came suddenly, after a routine physical revealed alarming blood work. What followed was a year of hospitalizations, chemotherapy rounds, and two bone marrow transplants. Thuan spent every night in a vinyl recliner beside his son’s bed, listening to the rhythmic beep of the IV pump and the hiss of the oxygen concentrator. The smell of antiseptic—a sharp, chemical scent that seemed to coat everything—became the permanent background of his life. He watched his son’s body shrink, watched the color drain from his face, watched the doctors come and go with their clipboards and their careful, neutral expressions. His son survived, eventually achieving remission, but something in Thuan had not survived the year intact.

In the months after his son came home, Thuan noticed that the smell of rubbing alcohol or hand sanitizer could stop him cold. He would be walking through the grocery store, reach for a cart, and suddenly the antiseptic odor would hit him—and he would be back in the hospital room, watching the bag of platelets drip, hearing the soft alarm of a pump that needed attention. His chest would tighten, his palms would sweat, and he would feel a surge of pure, animal fear, as though his son’s life was ending in that exact moment, all over again. He learned to avoid hospitals, declining his own annual physicals and ignoring the dental cleanings he had once kept like clockwork. When his daughter announced her pregnancy, he felt a jolt of dread so physical that he had to excuse himself from the dinner table. Babies, pregnancy, childbirth—all of it now felt like a doorway to the same corridor of waiting and watching. He could not explain why. When she tried to talk to him about her due date or her nausea, he would lose the thread mid-sentence, the words dissolving into images of his son’s pale hand against the white hospital sheets. The memory felt less like a recollection and more like a recurring event—a film that played behind his eyes without his permission, always the same scenes, always the same helplessness.

At work, Thuan had always been known for his methodical calm, the way he could trace a breach through layers of code without flinching. But now, the same analytical mind that had served him so well became a trap. He found himself replaying the diagnosis conversation in his head—the doctor’s careful phrasing, the way his son had looked at the ceiling—and each time, the replay brought the same raw horror, as if he were hearing it for the first time. He began to avoid meetings where medical leave or health insurance was discussed. He stopped going to the break room, where someone might be eating hospital-scented crackers or using a hand sanitizer dispenser. His colleagues noticed he had grown short-tempered, that he left the office the moment the clock struck five, that he no longer joined them for after-work drinks. He had come to believe that if he let his guard down, if he stopped monitoring the world for reminders, the fear would overwhelm him completely. He was certain that his body was betraying him, that the physical reactions—the racing heart, the nausea, the feeling of being smothered—were signs that he was about to lose control, maybe collapse, maybe die, just as he had feared his son would die.

What finally brought Thuan to seek help was a moment of public shame. During a routine cybersecurity audit at a hospital—a contract he could not refuse—he walked past an open supply closet and caught a wave of antiseptic smell. He froze in the hallway, his vision tunneling, his hands shaking, unable to speak or move. A young nurse touched his arm and asked if he was okay, and he could not answer. He could only stand there, lost in a memory that felt more real than the corridor around him. His daughter drove him to the appointment the next week. Thuan is not sure what he hopes for. He knows he cannot keep avoiding doctors, cannot keep dodging his daughter’s pregnancy, cannot keep leaving meetings early. But what frightens him most is the possibility that talking about it will only make the film play louder, that the memory will finally swallow him whole.
